title: What makes an AI-based game feel like a real game, rather than just an AI chatbot?
author: fwackedbubbed
selftext:
I’ve been thinking about this question while playing AI-based games.  
What I find interesting is that adding AI to a game doesn’t necessarily make it feel like a game. Even though AI characters can converse naturally, generate images, or react to your actions, sometimes the experience still feels more like chatting with an AI than actually playing a game.  
I’m really curious to know where everyone thinks that line is drawn.  
Is it about having a world that continues to exist beyond the conversation? Is it about having meaningful consequences? Or is it about having characters with their own motivations? Are there other factors that make an AI-generated experience feel like a real game?  
For developers who are working on AI games or experimenting with AI in their games, what do you think is the biggest difference between an AI chatbot with game elements and an actual AI-powered game?

comments.author: bcalmnrolldice

comments.author: Chaibi_Alaa
comments.body: Polishing, details, story, UX, coordination and logic.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
r/gamedesign

The answer is actual game design. AI gamedevs get the results without the process. So it feels lifeless, same with prompting an image.

I'm a gamedev for twenty years and oppose the idea of these infinite AI generated games. That's lifeless. AI generating text and images, then getting curated by a designer, perfectly fine. 

Usually the stakes are too low. You go into a dungeon and the AI keeps generating content. Sure but why? What's the goal? It just... generates.

replies.author: fwackedbubbed
replies.body:
Yeah, the “what’s the goal?” part really hits it for me.  
If the game can just keep generating more rooms, characters and events forever, that sounds cool for a while, but eventually I’d probably start wondering why I’m doing any of it.  
I think I’d rather have AI working inside something that already has a clear direction, instead of letting it generate the whole game endlessly.

comments.author: Fickle_Appearance558
comments.body: What ai based games?  Like made with ai or using ai within the game? I have a character harness that is like chatting mixed with parts of the sims as far as moods and relationships and becoming different over time goes, a common room for the characters to chat, character art that the model swaps per message, they search the web alone or by request, the self reflect and make plans and goals and check them off.  .  Ai in actual games at this point could house maybe npc characters that have actual lore and such to talk or be asked about.  Certain types of games could be tacked on to an ai chat app.  But i dont think we really have what you are thinking about yet.  My thing would be pretty boring or slow without api credits or a 16gb gpu.  A game with generated characters and worlds on the fly is right now, too expensive to run anything meaningfull. Best you can get is like shitty dungeons and dragons type chat games.  Did you find anything good?  Let me know, because it is interesting.

replies.author: fwackedbubbed
replies.body:
That’s actually pretty close to the problem I’ve been thinking about.A lot of AI RPG stuff does end up feeling like D&D-flavored chat with some extra systems around it. I’m more interested in whether things like persistent relationships, characters acting on their own, world state changing, and playing together with friends can push it past that.  
I haven’t really found one that fully nails it yet though.

comments.author: TonyDaDesigner
comments.body: i've tested using LLMs to guide NPC dialogue with mixed results.  When it comes to your question, I think the real question is: "What is the purpose of the NPC/dialogue?"  In MOST cases, Dialogue rarely adds "fun" to a game- it's usually there to guide a player's actions or provide context to a game's story.  I generally think excessive dialogue ruins more games than it helps, especially in the modern era.  You can definitely set up a small model with a good system prompt (and maybe even post-training) to converse with players and react to their actions, but I'd ask yourself \*why\* before getting too into the thick of it.  Also, FWIW, you really need to carefully test and manage your model because too much (or mismanaged) context or bad setup will ruin your outputs easily.   I ended up shelving my project with this idea because I found it to be a lot better by just using the LLM to create more canned dialogue options and variations.. ie. if you need to talk to an NPC to get 'information' you can just pre-generate a hundred different possible responses/variations- you'll have a lot more control and predictability over the interaction without both hogging resources and risking bad outputs.

replies.author: TonyDaDesigner
replies.body: and just to reiterate, most gamers aren't playing games because they want to talk to NPCs. there's really nothing exciting about it and most games that rely on this mechanic are boring

replies.author: fwackedbubbed
replies.body:
The part about NPC dialogue taking over the game is interesting. I’ve definitely had that feeling with some AI games where I realize I’ve spent 20 minutes just talking and basically nothing has happened.  
I like the idea of keeping the conversation tied to something concrete the player is trying to do. Maybe the NPC remembers it, reacts later, changes what they do, or opens up a different way forward. Otherwise it’s really easy for the whole thing to turn into a chat app with game UI around it.

Your point about shorter responses makes sense too. I hadn’t really thought about response length as part of the game design itself.

comments.author: pablo603
comments.body: The same things that make a regular good game a good game.

comments.author: SnuffleBag
comments.body:
Nobody knows. There is not a single one in existence.

But the answer is: the same things that make a traditionally developed game feel like a real game.
